Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural primary healthcare clinics
Comments: Rural primary healthcare clinics (Area Health Centres, Medi-Clinics, Community Health Centres) in Mauritius predominantly use paper-based recording for patient data. Government audits confirm failed implementations of digital systems like IPCS at these facilities, with hardware unused and records kept manually as of 2016.Mauritius Audit Report WHO's 2015 report notes no EMR/EHR at primary level, reliant on paper forms.WHO He@lth 2015 As of Feb 2025, the system remains mostly paper-based per UNDP roadmap, with the 'One Patient, One Record' PAS/EHR project in early rollout: piloting at one regional hospital, planned extension to health centers/mediclinics/community centers (Phase 1), but not yet standard at point of service.UNDP Roadmap No evidence of majority rural adoption; represents donor/govt project akin to score 2. Barriers: IT infrastructure gaps, staff training, business process re-engineering, past system failures. National ambition (eHealth strategy) outpaces rural reality, where paper persists for daily recording, with possible aggregate reporting digital.

revision_notes: Confirmed score of 1 (Entirely paper). Newest evidence: Ministry of Health and Wellness Annual Report FY2024-2025 (October 2025) and Le Defi Media (August 2025) confirm the e-Health/PAS rollout remains at pilot/testing stage at one hospital (Sir Anerood Jugnauth National Hospital) and two partner clinics, with no evidence of digital data capture extended to rural Area Health Centres, Medi-Clinics or Community Health Centres. The original 2016/2017 National Audit Office report and 2015 WHO source remain directionally consistent with continued reliance on paper at the facility level. Score confirmed unchanged.
revised_comments: Rural primary healthcare clinics (Area Health Centres, Medi-Clinics and Community Health Centres) in Mauritius continue to rely almost entirely on paper-based patient records at the point of care. The Ministry of Health and Wellness's "One Patient, One Record" e-Health project, supported by UNDP, remains in its early pilot phase: as at mid-2025 the Patient Administration System module was undergoing testing solely at the Sir Anerood Jugnauth National Hospital's Unsorted Outpatient Department and two partner clinics (Belvédère and Bel Air), with training limited to hospital records officers. Extension to Area Health Centres, Community Health Centres and Mediclinics is planned but has not yet occurred, so data capture at rural facilities themselves remains paper-based.

Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural primary schools
Comments: Mauritius has deployed OpenEMIS for education data management at national, zonal, and school levels, with UNESCO capacity building in 2022 following 2019 needs assessment and SIMIS design. All primary schools have high-speed internet (pre-2020). Government publishes detailed digital enrollment data by grade/gender. Recent AI tools like mytGPT piloted in primary schools for real-time monitoring. Digital Mauritius 2030 and reforms aim for full sector digitalisation, including student tracking. No evidence of paper-based recording at rural primaries; EMIS implies direct digital entry at schools. Rodrigues (rural) included in pilots/data. As upper-middle income, predominantly digital with possible legacy paper in remote areas.

revision_notes: Confirmed score of 3 (Mostly digital - some paper). Newest verifiable evidence dates to 2022 (UNESCO IITE OpenEMIS capacity-building webinars for Ministry staff at national, zonal and school level) and 2019 (UNESCO EMIS needs assessment and design mission, which explicitly describes facility-level automation visits to primary and secondary schools). This satisfies the metadata's requirement that scoring reflect data capture at the facility itself, not just central aggregation. No 2023-2025 source was found confirming continued or expanded school-level digital capture, so the evidence is somewhat dated; no basis was found to promote to 4 (Entirely digital), as elimination of all paper processes at rural primary schools is not evidenced.
revised_comments: Mauritius operates OpenEMIS as its Education Management Information System, with data entered and managed directly at national, zonal and school level. Following a 2019 EMIS needs assessment and design mission and a 2022 UNESCO-supported capacity-building programme for Ministry of Education staff, school-level administrators use OpenEMIS modules to record student and staff profiles, attendance, enrolment and academic performance. All government primary schools, including those in Rodrigues, have had high-speed internet connectivity since before 2020, supporting direct digital data entry at the school level rather than reliance on central re-keying of paper forms. Some paper-based classroom processes likely persist alongside the digital system, consistent with a "mostly digital, some paper" status for rural primary schools.

Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural police stations
Comments: Mauritius Police Force (MPF) maintains a centralized digital Criminal Attribute Database (CADB) at Crime Records Office (CRO) for convictions and fingerprints, with 12,457 electronic fingerprint submissions from 7 remote workstations including Rodrigues (rural island) in 2023-24 MPF Annual Report 2023-2024. Police IT Unit handles digital forensics (2,034 exams), CCTV integration via Safe City/PMCCC, and network support across force MPF Annual Report 2023-2024. Certificate of Character (criminal record check) available online via portal, processed at DHQs including rural areas police.govmu.org. However, case dockets (PF forms) and outstanding cases (91k crimes) suggest initial paper recording at 72 stations (many rural/peripheral), with data uploaded centrally. No evidence of full digital case/incident logging at rural stations; hybrid model predominant: paper-based locally, digital aggregates/pilots centrally. GIS/CCTV limited to urban (Port Louis/Grand Bay). Score 2 fits predominantly paper with some digital (central reporting, pilots).

revision_notes: Confirmed score of 2 (Mostly paper - some digital). Newer evidence: a Prime Minister's statement to the National Assembly, reported 18 June 2025, confirms all police stations have computers used for the Crime Occurrence Tracking System (COTS, introduced 2011) and terminals accessing the Criminal Attribute Database (CADB, operational since 1999), but both systems are ageing and slated for replacement (Rs 43 million allocated in the 2025-2026 budget, tender from end-August 2025). This supersedes but is directionally consistent with the MPF Annual Report 2023-2024 previously cited, and confirms continued hybrid paper/digital station-level operations rather than full digitisation. Score confirmed unchanged.
revised_comments: Rural police stations in Mauritius operate a hybrid model combining paper-based station records with long-standing central digital systems. All stations are equipped with computers used for the Crime Occurrence Tracking System (COTS, introduced in 2011) for tracking complaints, and terminals accessing the Criminal Attribute Database (CADB, operational since 1999) for criminal records and fingerprint management. As at mid-2025 both systems remain in force-wide use but are dated: government has allocated Rs 43 million in the 2025-2026 budget to replace COTS with a new case management system and to modernise CADB with biometric capability, with a tender process beginning at the end of August 2025. Daily station-level records such as occurrence books and case dockets remain predominantly paper-based, with digital systems chiefly supporting centralised case tracking and criminal record-keeping rather than full point-of-entry digitisation, consistent with a "mostly paper, some digital" status.

Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural civil registry offices
Comments: Rural registry offices in Mauritius likely rely predominantly on paper-based processes for birth registration, with parents appearing at district Civil Status Offices to submit documents (hospital attestation, IDs, etc.) and sign a physical register, as per the official government process description with no mention of on-site digital entry.Civil Status Division A 2012 UNECA report notes 47 total offices, 32 fully computerized for instant digital entry, and 15 non-computerized using manual entry forms transferred to computerized sites for data entry—non-computerized offices are plausibly the more remote/rural ones given Mauritius' small size and centralized structure.UNECA CRVS Report Data reaches central electronic Central Population Database and Statistics Mauritius monthly in digital format, indicating aggregation rather than point-of-service digitalisation. No recent rural-specific evidence found of predominant digital shift; online access exists for certificates via Mokloud, but not registration. Mauritius has strong overall CRVS (complete per older sources), but rural facilities appear to use paper as default with digital support centrally. Key barriers: legacy non-computerized remote offices, potential infrastructure limits. National policy emphasizes digital gov (e.g., Digital Mauritius 2030), but rural point-of-service lags, fitting score 2 (pilots/digital in some, paper predominant).

revision_notes: Score of 2 (Mostly paper - some digital) confirmed but the evidence base is ageing: the only source located that specifically breaks down computerised versus non-computerised offices is the UNECA CRVS country report (approximately 2012), which found 32 of 47 offices fully computerised for instant registration and the remainder using manual entry forms later transferred for central data entry. No more recent breakdown of office-level computerisation was located despite dedicated searching. The current Civil Status Division office list (csd.govmu.org, 2024) shows a rationalised network of around 38 offices, including several small part-time rural sub-offices (open only two or three days a week), but does not state their computerisation status. Given Mauritius has since undertaken substantial digital identity and e-government modernisation (Mokloud online certificates from 2021, MNIC Portal 3.0), but no source confirms this has extended to point-of-service digitisation in all rural civil status offices, this row is flagged for human review.
revised_comments: Mauritius's Civil Status Division operates under the Civil Status Act 1981 (as amended) through a network of around 38 offices, comprising the Central Civil Status Office, 34 sub-offices across the island of Mauritius, two offices in Rodrigues and one in Agalega. Historically, only a subset of these offices has been fully computerised with instant, on-site digital registration; the remainder, plausibly including smaller part-time rural sub-offices open only two or three days a week, record entries manually on paper forms that are then transferred to a computerised office for data entry into the central Civil Status Database. Certificates are generated instantly only at computerised offices, while non-computerised offices route documents through a computerised office before returning them to the applicant. Aggregate vital statistics are compiled centrally in electronic format on a monthly basis regardless of the point-of-service recording method used at individual offices.
